kernelIdea: (g∘f)(s) = g(f(s)) is defined when the codomain of f is the domain of g. Composition preserves injectivity and preserves surjectivity.

kernels.l1: Two machines in a row make one bigger machine.
kernels.l2: You can run one machine and then feed its answer into another. This only works if the second machine takes what the first one gives out.
kernels.l3: Doing f and then g gives a new function, written g ∘ f, and read right to left. It is only defined when the answers of f are things g can take.
kernels.l4: (g ∘ f)(s) = g(f(s)) is defined when the codomain of f is the domain of g. If f and g are both injective so is g ∘ f, and if both are surjective so is g ∘ f.
kernels.l5: Composition is defined when codomain meets domain; it preserves injectivity and surjectivity, and the partial converses are worth knowing.
kernels.l6: Composition is associative with the identity as unit, and it preserves injectivity and surjectivity separately.
kernels.l7: g ∘ f is defined when the codomain of f equals the domain of g; composition preserves injectivity and surjectivity, and satisfies partial converses that identify which factor must be well behaved.
kernels.l8: Composition is the associative operation making Set a category; identities are units, and preservation of mono and epi under composition is a categorical fact, not a set-theoretic one.

kernel: (g∘f)(s) = g(f(s)) is defined when f's codomain is g's domain. Composition preserves injectivity and preserves surjectivity.
objectives: Prove that the composition of injections is an injection
